Troubleshooting#

Answers to the failures that look alarming but are expected, each with the page that explains the behavior.

Why did the scheduled refresh-patches job fail?#

A scheduled refresh-patches failure is expected whenever upstream ships a patch. The scheduled job is check-only: when the policy changed, the tool exits 3 and the job fails on the diff. Treat the red run as a to-do, not an outage. On GitLab the policy robot's Monday run usually lands the same patch on main by itself (or, in a red week, carries it in its fallback merge request): check main first. Otherwise run php bin/refresh-patches.php, read the diff, run composer ci, add a CHANGELOG line, and commit. The Changelog is where that line goes.

Why does the policy-bot job print "CREED_BOT_TOKEN not set; skipping the policy robot" and stay green?#

That is the designed behavior when the masked CREED_BOT_TOKEN CI variable is not set: the job prints the line and stays green. Missing CI variables stop the run before any push, so nothing is committed. The job runs on its dedicated schedule (the one carrying CREED_JOB=policy-bot) and by hand from the web. It landed in 0.1.6; see the Changelog.

Why can the robot not push when auto/policy-refresh is protected?#

The branch auto/policy-refresh must not be protected, or the robot cannot push it. It is the red-week fallback: when composer ci fails on the refresh, the robot force-pushes the commit there as a merge request labeled auto-data. A green week pushes to main with the job token instead, which needs "Allow Git push requests to the repository" (CI/CD > Job token permissions) and a schedule owner who may push to the protected main. Branch protection is a project setting, not a file in this repo; The policy robot has the whole setup.

Why did the robot open a merge request instead of pushing to main?#

Because the gate went red, on purpose. The robot runs composer ci on its refresh in its own job, and only a green gate pushes straight to main. A red one force-pushes the commit to auto/policy-refresh as a merge request labeled auto-data and fails the job, so the schedule owner gets mail. The failure may have nothing to do with the policy (a fresh security advisory in composer audit, say). Read the failed job, fix the failure on main, then start the robot by hand on main: a green gate pushes the refresh itself, and the stale merge request can be closed. Held and refused items are in the body and each still has an auto-alert issue, red or green. Never commit to auto/policy-refresh: the next red run overwrites it. Reviewing what it does walks through it.

Tests fail oddly on Windows after a Docker install#

Delete vendor/ and install again. The install and Docker paths are in Install.

composer ci fails because the docs site or handbook site is stale#

Rebuild the stale side: composer docs rebuilds the docs site from docs/, and composer site:handbook rebuilds the handbook site. Proof covers what composer ci checks, including the stale-page failure.

What is the difference between refresh-policy exit 3 and exit 4?#

Exit 3 means something was written to policy/policy.json or policy/sources.json, including a released loosen-fail (the policy robot raises the alert from the report). Exit 4 means something was held or refused: whatever could be written was written, the held or refused items stayed out, and the policy robot runs its gate on whatever was written, as for exit 3, with an auto-alert issue per held or refused item. The refresher itself never commits. Exit 0 means nothing worth committing, and exit 1 is a hard failure. Version 0.1.2 changed a released loosening from exit 4 to exit 3; see the Changelog.

Why does the reader throw for a version between listed lines, or one that does not parse?#

The reader refuses what it does not know, except the newest thing and the oldest. A version that sorts above every line the policy lists is Active, and a version that parses and sorts below every listed line is Eol, with the reason from belowOldestLineReason(). A version that falls between listed lines, or that does not parse, is still unknown, and still throws. Unlisted components are refused the same way. Current versions are never refused. The handbook's Dependencies chapter explains the states.

Creed Bratton would not care, but he is not reviewing the merge request.
